lesson.title: Mapping the Terrain: Building a Sign Chart
lesson.summary: A sign chart is a number line marked with a function's critical numbers that records the sign of the derivative on each resulting interval, turning the First Derivative Test into a fast, visual, and far less error prone procedure.
lesson.body:
Building a sign chart follows four steps. First, find every critical number of f, from both f'(x) = 0 and f'(x) undefined, keeping only values inside the domain of f, and mark each one on a number line in increasing order. Second, notice that these critical numbers divide the number line into a set of open intervals. Third, in each interval, pick any single convenient test value and evaluate only the sign, positive or negative, of f' there, since the exact size of f' does not matter for classification, only whether it is above or below zero. Fourth, read the classification straight off the chart using the First Derivative Test rules: positive to negative is a local maximum, negative to positive is a local minimum, and no change is neither.

The chart earns its keep once there are more than two critical numbers to juggle, since keeping several sign changes straight in your head is genuinely error prone, and it is especially good at making the no change case, easy to miss by accident, visually obvious instead of easy to overlook.

Work through f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3. Its derivative is f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2, which factors as f'(x) = 4x^2(x - 3). Setting this equal to zero: 4x^2(x - 3) = 0, which happens when x^2 = 0, giving x = 0, or when x - 3 = 0, giving x = 3. The domain of f is every real number, so both values are valid critical numbers, giving exactly two distinct critical numbers even though x = 0 arises from a repeated factor.

Mark 0 and 3 on the number line. They split it into three intervals: (-infinity, 0), (0, 3), and (3, infinity). Test x = -1 in the first interval: f'(-1) = 4(-1)^2(-1 - 3) = 4(1)(-4) = -16, negative. Test x = 1 in the second interval: f'(1) = 4(1)^2(1 - 3) = 4(1)(-2) = -8, negative. Test x = 4 in the third interval: f'(4) = 4(4)^2(4 - 3) = 4(16)(1) = 64, positive. The completed chart reads: negative on (-infinity, 0), negative on (0, 3), positive on (3, infinity).

Now classify each critical number using the chart. At x = 0, the sign goes from negative to negative, no change at all, so x = 0 is a critical number that is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum, just a brief flattening of the tangent line on the way down, since the x^2 factor touches zero without changing the overall negative sign contributed by the (x - 3) factor. At x = 3, the sign goes from negative to positive, so f has a local minimum at x = 3, with value f(3) = 3^4 - 4(3)^3 = 81 - 108 = -27.

This example is worth sitting with, because it is exactly the scenario a sign chart is built to catch. Without laying the signs out visually, it is tempting to assume every critical number automatically produces a peak or a valley, especially after seeing the clean two-extrema example from the previous section. The chart makes the exception at x = 0 impossible to miss. That closes the loop running through this entire sequence: a critical point is only ever a candidate, never a guarantee, whether it arises from a horizontal tangent or from a derivative that fails to exist, and the sign chart, built from the First Derivative Test, is the tool that turns the candidate list into a final, verified answer.
